learn: Tree representation as a disjunction of conjunctions
Worked ID3 on EnjoySport and PlayTennis
Evaluation and prediction; pros, cons and applications
Continuous attributes: multi-way and binary splits with Gini
Gini index, gain ratio and split information
Minimum Description Length and its link to MAP
intro.why: Trees are interpretable, handle mixed data, and are the base learners of random forests and gradient boosting. The impurity and pruning ideas here recur throughout ML.

symbols: set of training examples at a node

sections.title: Representation and expressiveness
sections.plain: Paths are conjunctions; the tree is their disjunction.
sections.body:
Decision trees are discriminative, rule-based classifiers. Example: Home Owner (binary), Marital Status (categorical), Annual Income (continuous) → Defaulted Borrower (class), with trees of increasing size (a)–(d).

A tree represents a disjunction of conjunctions of attribute constraints: $$(\text{Outlook}=\text{Sunny}\wedge\text{Humidity}=\text{Normal})\vee(\text{Outlook}=\text{Overcast})\vee(\text{Outlook}=\text{Rain}\wedge\text{Wind}=\text{Weak}).$$ Classify $\langle$Sunny, Hot, High, Strong$\rangle$ by following Sunny → Humidity = High → No.

sections.title: Measure of information
sections.body: The information (surprise) of a message is inversely related to its probability: $I_k\propto\frac1{p_k}$. The logarithm satisfies the required properties (additivity for independent events, zero for certain events): $$I_k=\log_2\frac1{p_k}\ \text{bits}.$$

sections.title: Entropy
sections.plain: Expected information; impurity of a set.
sections.body:
$$H(X)=\mathbb E[I(X)]=\mathbb E[-\log P(X)]=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}P(x_i)\log_2P(x_i).$$

As uncertainty increases, entropy increases. Binary: $H=-p_+\log_2p_+-p_-\log_2p_-$. For $c$ classes $H=-\sum_{i=1}^cp_i\log_2p_i=\sum p_i\log_2\frac1{p_i}$, with $0\le H\le\log_2c$.

Examples, with $0\log_20=0$: $H([14+,0-])=0$; $H([9+,5-])=-\frac9{14}\log_2\frac9{14}-\frac5{14}\log_2\frac5{14}=0.940$; $H([7+,7-])=1$.

sections.title: Worked problem: EnjoySport (problem types 1–2)
sections.plain: Compute entropies, pick the zero-entropy attribute.
sections.body:
Four training days (Sky, AirTemp, Humidity, Wind, Forecast → EnjoySport): Sunny Warm Normal Strong Same Yes; Sunny Warm High Strong Same Yes; Rainy Cold High Strong Change No; Sunny Warm High Strong Change Yes. $H(S)=H(3,1)=0.811$ (a commonly quoted version writes 0.4421 + 0.5 = 0.94).

AttributeWeighted child entropy
Sky$\frac34H(3,0)+\frac14H(0,1)=0$
AirTemp0
Humidity$\frac14\cdot0+\frac34H(2,1)=0.689$
Wind$1\cdot H(3,1)=0.811$
Forecast$\frac24\cdot0+\frac24\cdot1=0.5$

Sky and AirTemp give pure children (highest gain); either yields an equally correct tree: Sky = Sunny → Yes, Rainy → No. Class balancing is recommended before building; for $k$ classes entropy ranges from 0 to $\log_2k$.

Problem type 2: if a node is heterogeneous, continue on that subset. Convergence: all training data learnt, no more learning possible, or hyperparameter constraints satisfied.

sections.title: Information gain on PlayTennis
sections.body:
$$\text{Gain}(S,A)=H(S)-\sum_{v\in\text{Values}(A)}\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)$$

Maximising gain = minimising the weighted average impurity of children.

Wind: $S=[9+,5-]$, $S_{\text{Weak}}=[6+,2-]$, $S_{\text{Strong}}=[3+,3-]$: $$\text{Gain}=0.940-\tfrac8{14}(0.811)-\tfrac6{14}(1.00)=0.048.$$ Humidity: High $[3+,4-]$ $H=0.985$, Normal $[6+,1-]$ $H=0.592$: $0.940-\frac7{14}0.985-\frac7{14}0.592=0.151$.

Root choice: Gain(Outlook) = 0.246, Humidity 0.151, Wind 0.048, Temperature 0.029 → Outlook. Branches: Sunny $\{D1,D2,D8,D9,D11\}[2+,3-]$, Overcast $\{D3,D7,D12,D13\}[4+,0-]$ → Yes, Rain $\{D4,D5,D6,D10,D14\}[3+,2-]$.

sections.title: Growing the tree and the ID3 algorithm
sections.plain: Recurse on each branch with the remaining attributes.
sections.body:
Sunny node, $H=0.970$: Gain(Humidity) $=0.970-\frac35(0)-\frac25(0)=0.970$; Gain(Temp) $=0.970-\frac25(0)-\frac25(1)-\frac15(0)=0.570$; Gain(Wind) $=0.970-\frac25(1.0)-\frac35(0.918)=0.019$ → Humidity. Rain node → Wind. Final tree: Sunny→Humidity (High: No, Normal: Yes), Overcast: Yes, Rain→Wind (Strong: No, Weak: Yes).

Stopping: all samples at the node share a class; no attributes remain (use majority voting); no samples left.

ID3(X, T, Attrs)                 # X examples, T target, Attrs candidate attributes
  create Root
  if all X are +: return Root labelled +
  if all X are −: return Root labelled −
  if Attrs is empty: return Root labelled with most common T in X
  A ← attribute in Attrs with highest Gain(X, A)
  for each value v of A:
      add branch A = v;  X_v ← {x ∈ X : A = v}
      if X_v empty: add leaf with most common T in X
      else: add subtree ID3(X_v, T, Attrs − {A})
  return Root

Supplementary Cost: computing all gains at a node is $O(n\,d)$ for $n$ examples and $d$ categorical attributes; a balanced tree has $O(\log n)$ levels, so building is roughly $O(n\,d\log n)$; prediction is $O(\text{depth})$.

sections.title: Prediction and evaluation (problem types 3–4)
sections.plain: Follow the path; evaluate on unseen data.
sections.body:
Problem type 3: predict $\langle$Rainy, Warm, Normal, Breeze, Same$\rangle$ with the Sky tree → No; predict $\langle$Sunny, Hot, High, Weak$\rangle$ with the PlayTennis tree → Sunny, High → No.

Problem type 4: evaluation as in Module 4 (confusion matrix $CM_{i,j}$ = tuples of class $i$ labelled $j$). Quality is judged on unseen validation/test instances; training performance only for comparison. The test row (Rainy, Warm, Normal, Breeze, Same → Yes) is misclassified by the Sky tree.

sections.title: Advantages, disadvantages and applications
sections.plain: Cheap and readable, but greedy and axis-aligned.
sections.body:
Advantages: inexpensive to construct; extremely fast at classifying; easy to interpret for small trees; handle redundant or irrelevant attributes (unless interacting). Disadvantages: the space of trees is exponentially large; greedy approaches often miss the best tree; interactions between attributes are not modelled directly; each boundary involves one attribute (axis-parallel).

Suited when instances are attribute–value pairs, targets are discrete, disjunctive descriptions are needed, and data may have missing values. Applications: biomedical, manufacturing, banking, make-or-buy decisions.

sections.title: Continuous attributes (problem types 5–6)
sections.plain: Create A_c = (A < c) and search c.
sections.body:
Example trees with thresholds: Humidity > 75%, Wind > 20. Split types: binary vs multi-way, for nominal (Marital Status), ordinal (Shirt Size, keeping order) and continuous attributes (Annual Income > 80K, or ranges).

Create $A_c=\text{True}$ if $AWay 1, multi-way: sort by the attribute; candidate thresholds are midpoints where the class changes. Temperature 40 48 | 60 72 80 | 90 with PlayTennis No No Yes Yes Yes No gives $c=(48+60)/2=54$ and $(80+90)/2=85$.

Way 2, binary split by Gini: sort Annual Income (60, 70, 75, 85, 90, 95, 100, 120, 125, 220K), scan split positions 55, 65, 72.5, …, 230, compute class counts on each side and the weighted Gini; minimum 0.300 at 97.5K.

sections.title: Overfitting in decision trees
sections.plain: Noise forces extra splits that don't generalise.
sections.body:
A new noisy example $\langle$Sunny, Hot, Normal, Strong, No$\rangle$ forces an extra split under Sunny/Normal. Overfitting: too many branches reflect anomalies (noise, outliers), giving poor accuracy on unseen samples. Approaches: pruning; constraints on depth; minimum examples per leaf.

ID3 on the shape/colour/size → action data grows an over-fit tree (Shape → Square → Size → Big → Colour → …) that misclassifies the validation set.

sections.title: Pre-pruning and post-pruning (problem types 7–8)
sections.plain: Stop early by a gain threshold, or cut back with a prune set.
sections.body:
Pre-pruning: threshold Gain ≤ 0.85. Under Shape = Square the best gain is 0.8113 (= entropy of [3 Allow, 1 Reject], fully resolved by Size) ≤ 0.85, so stop and assign the majority "Allow". Under Oval the best gain is 0.9182 (Colour) > 0.85, so split: Green → Reject, Brown → Allow. A pruned leaf uses majority voting; a tree can also estimate class-membership probabilities from leaf proportions.

Post-pruning, on an intermediate tree (Square → Size; Oval → Colour): error rate = % of tuples misclassified on a prune set. Procedure: scan bottom-up; at each decision node evaluate the tree with and without the node on the prune set; if removing it (replacing it by its majority leaf) reduces the error, prune; else keep; repeat for the other branches. In the prune set, replacing the Colour node by a majority leaf changes the predictions shown in the green columns.

Supplementary scikit-learn implements cost-complexity pruning: minimise $R(T)+\alpha|\text{leaves}(T)|$, choosing $\alpha$ by validation (see code).

sections.title: Tree size vs error: model comparison (problem type 9)
sections.plain: Training error keeps falling; test error turns up.
sections.body:
Two-class data: + 5,200 instances (5,000 from a Gaussian at (10,10) plus 200 noise points), o 5,200 uniform; 10% for training, 90% for testing. As nodes increase from 1 to ~150, training error falls from ~0.48 to ~0. A 4-node tree draws one box around the centre; a 50-node tree carves many small boxes around noise.

Underfitting: model too simple, both errors large. Overfitting: model too complex, training error small but test error large. Our reproduction in code: test error is lowest around 8–16 leaves and rises to 0.22 for the fully grown tree.

sections.title: Gini index for binary splits
sections.plain: 1 − Σ p²; pick the split with lowest weighted Gini.
sections.body:
$$\text{Gini}(t)=1-\sum_{i=0}^{c-1}p_i(t)^2,\qquad I(\text{children})=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{N(v_j)}{N}I(v_j).$$

Parent (7 No, 3 Yes): $1-(0.3)^2-(0.7)^2=0.420$. Home owner: N1 (Yes) = [0 Yes, 3 No] Gini 0; N2 (No) = [3 Yes, 4 No] Gini $1-(3/7)^2-(4/7)^2=0.490$; weighted $\frac3{10}\cdot0+\frac7{10}\cdot0.490=0.343$; gain $0.420-0.343=0.077$.

Marital status: {Single} | {Married, Divorced} 0.400; {Single, Married} | {Divorced} 0.400; {Single, Divorced} | {Married} 0.343. Home owner and the last marital split are the best candidates (lowest weighted Gini).

sections.title: Gain ratio and split information (problem type 10)
sections.plain: Divide gain by the entropy of the partition sizes.
sections.body:
$$\text{SplitInformation}(S,A)=-\sum_{i=1}^{c}\frac{|S_i|}{|S|}\log_2\frac{|S_i|}{|S|},\qquad \text{GainRatio}(S,A)=\frac{\text{Gain}(S,A)}{\text{SplitInformation}(S,A)}.$$

SplitInformation is the entropy of $S$ with respect to the values of $A$: the more uniformly dispersed, the higher. A Date-like attribute splitting $n$ examples into $n$ singletons has SplitInfo $=\log_2n$; a balanced binary attribute has 1.

Problem type 10, 20 customers (10 C0, 10 C1), parent entropy 1:

AttributeChild entropyGainSplitInfoGain ratio
Gender0.9710.02910.029
Car type0.3800.6201.520.41
Customer ID014.320.23

Customer ID has the highest information gain but a lower gain ratio than Car type, which is chosen.

sections.title: Minimum Description Length (problem type 11)
sections.plain: Minimise bits for the tree plus bits for its errors.
sections.body:
From MAP: $$h_{MAP}=\arg\max_hP(D\mid h)P(h)=\arg\min_h\left[-\log_2P(D\mid h)-\log_2P(h)\right].$$ The optimal code for an event of probability $p$ has length $-\log_2p$ bits, so $-\log_2P(h)=L_{C_1}(h)$ (bits to encode the model) and $-\log_2P(D\mid h)=L_{C_2}(D\mid h)$ (bits to encode the data's errors given the model). MDL: $$h_{MDL}=\arg\min_{h\in H}L_{C_1}(h)+L_{C_2}(D\mid h).$$ For trees: $L_{C_1}$ = bits to describe the tree; $L_{C_2}=0$ if all examples are classified correctly, otherwise only exceptions are encoded. MDL trades tree size for training errors (Occam's razor), one remedy for overfitting.

Problem type 11: 16 binary attributes, 3 classes. Internal node cost $\log_2 16=4$ bits; leaf cost $\lceil\log_23\rceil=2$ bits; each error $\log_2n$ bits. Tree (a): 2 internal, 3 leaves, 7 errors → $2\cdot4+3\cdot2+7\log_2n=14+7\log_2n$. Tree (b): 4 internal, 5 leaves, 4 errors → $26+4\log_2n$. (a) is better iff $3\log_2n<12\iff n<16$; (b) for $n>16$.

sections.title: Comparisons, assumptions and misconceptions
sections.body:
ID3C4.5CART (scikit-learn)
CriterionInformation gainGain ratioGini (or entropy); MSE for regression
SplitsMulti-way, categoricalMulti-way; thresholds for numbersBinary only
PruningNoneError-based post-pruningCost-complexity
Missing valuesNoFractional instancesSurrogates (classic CART)
  • "Entropy and Gini give very different trees." They usually agree; Gini is slightly cheaper and favours isolating the largest class.
  • "Feature importance from a tree is reliable." Impurity-based importance is biased toward high-cardinality features; use permutation importance.
  • "Trees extrapolate." Predictions are constant outside the training range.
  • "Trees are stable." Small data changes can change the root and the whole tree; ensembles fix this (Module 9).

code.title: Gini splits, best income threshold and gain ratio
code.explain: Computes weighted Gini for each candidate split from the borrower table, scans income thresholds (best 97.5K, Gini 0.300), and reproduces the gain-ratio table.
mistakes: Choosing thresholds at observed values instead of midpoints.
code.code:
import numpy as np

gini = lambda counts: 1 - sum((c / sum(counts)) ** 2 for c in counts)
H = lambda counts: -sum(c / sum(counts) * np.log2(c / sum(counts)) for c in counts if c)

#: defaulted borrowers (No = 7, Yes = 3)
print("Gini(parent) =", round(gini([7, 3]), 3))
owner = np.array(["Y","N","N","Y","N","N","Y","N","N","N"])
marital = np.array(["S","M","S","M","D","S","D","S","M","S"])
y = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1])            # defaulted?
def wgini(mask):
    return sum(m.sum() / len(y) * gini([np.sum(y[m] == 0), np.sum(y[m] == 1)]) for m in (mask, ~mask))
splits = {"HomeOwner = Yes": owner == "Y", "Marital {Single} | {Married, Divorced}": marital == "S",
          "Marital {Married} | {Single, Divorced}": marital == "M", "Marital {Divorced} | {Single, Married}": marital == "D"}
for k, m in splits.items():
    print(f"{k:40s} weighted Gini = {wgini(m):.3f}  gain = {gini([7, 3]) - wgini(m):.3f}")

# Annual income: best binary threshold by Gini 
inc = np.array([125, 100, 70, 120, 95, 60, 220, 85, 75, 90])
s = np.sort(np.unique(inc)); cands = np.r_[s[0] - 5, (s[:-1] + s[1:]) / 2, s[-1] + 10]
best = []
for c in cands:
    L, R = y[inc <= c], y[inc > c]
    g = sum(len(p) / len(y) * gini([np.sum(p == 0), np.sum(p == 1)]) for p in (L, R) if len(p))
    best.append((round(g, 3), c))
print("Gini per threshold:", [(float(c), float(g)) for g, c in best]); print("best threshold:", float(min(best)[1]), "Gini", float(min(best)[0]))

# Gain ratio: 20 customers, classes C0/C1 10/10
for name, parts in {"Gender": [[6, 4], [4, 6]], "CarType": [[1, 3], [8, 0], [1, 7]], "CustomerID": [[1, 0]] * 10 + [[0, 1]] * 10}.items():
    n = 20; child = sum(sum(p) / n * H(p) for p in parts); g = 1 - child
    split = H([sum(p) for p in parts]); print(f"{name:10s} gain {g:.3f}  split info {split:.3f}  gain ratio {g / split:.3f}")

code.title: Overfitting and cost-complexity pruning
code.explain: Recreates the two-class experiment (10% train) and shows test error vs number of leaves, then prunes using a held-out prune set.
mistakes: Choosing ccp_alpha on the test set.
code.notes: In practice tune max_depth, min_samples_leaf or ccp_alpha with cross-validation.
code.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Like: '+' from a Gaussian at (10,10) plus noise, 'o' uniform on [0,20]^2; 10% train, 90% test
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pos = np.vstack([rng.normal(10, 2, (5000, 2)), rng.uniform(0, 20, (200, 2))])
neg = rng.uniform(0, 20, (5200, 2))
X = np.vstack([pos, neg]); y = np.r_[np.ones(5200), np.zeros(5200)]
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, train_size=0.1, random_state=0, stratify=y)

print("leaves  train_err  test_err")
for leaves in [2, 4, 8, 16, 50, 150, None]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_leaf_nodes=leaves, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{str(t.get_n_leaves()):>6}  {1 - t.score(X_tr, y_tr):9.3f}  {1 - t.score(X_te, y_te):8.3f}")

# Post-pruning: cost-complexity pruning path, choose alpha on a held-out prune set
X_a, X_p, y_a, y_p = train_test_split(X_tr, y_tr, test_size=0.3, random_state=1, stratify=y_tr)
path = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_a, y_a)
scores = [(DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=a, random_state=0).fit(X_a, y_a).score(X_p, y_p), a) for a in path.ccp_alphas]
acc, a = max(scores)
best = DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=a, random_state=0).fit(X_a, y_a)
print(f"pruned tree: {best.get_n_leaves()} leaves, test error {1 - best.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
